{{italic title}}
'''''The Design of Experiments''''' is a 1935 book by the English [[statistics|statistician]], [[Ronald Fisher]], on experimental design, considered to be a foundational work in modern statistics and experimental methodology.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Fisher |first=R. A. |url=http://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.502684 |title=The Design Of Experiments |date=January 1, 1935 |publisher=Oliver & Boyd Ltd. |isbn= |edition=1st |location=Edinburgh |publication-date= |pages=1–252 |language=en}}</ref> The book introduced concepts such as randomization, replication, blocking, and contains Fisher’s influential discussion of the [[null hypothesis]], illustrated in the context of the [[Lady tasting tea experiment]]. The book has had a lasting impact on the development of statistical science, shaping diverse fields such as agriculture, psychology, and medical research. It remains an important reference in the history of applied statistics and the philosophy of scientific testing.<ref name=":0" />

== Background ==
At the time of publication, Fisher was a statistician at [[Rothamsted Research]] (formally known as Rothamsted Experimental Station) where he developed statistical methods to analyze agricultural data.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Box |first=J. F. |date=February 1980 |title=R.A. Fisher and the Design of Experiments, 1922-1926 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2682986 |journal=The American Statistician |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=1–7 |doi=10.2307/2682986 |via=JSTOR|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His broader career included fundamental contributions to statistics, genetics, and evolutionary biology. ''The Design of Experiments'' built on Fisher’s earlier work, including his book ''[[Statistical Methods for Research Workers]]'' (1925), and laid the groundwork for the practical application of statistical tests in experimental science.<ref name=":0" />

Much of Fisher’s approach grew out of earlier studies at [[Rothamsted Research|Rothamsted]], particularly a 1923 paper with [[Winifred Mackenzie]] on crop variation.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Aldrich |first=J. |date=August 1997 |title=R. A. Fisher and the Making of Maximum Likelihood 1912-1922 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2246367 |journal=Statistical Science |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=162–176 |issn=0883-4237 |via=JSTOR}}</ref> In this work, Fisher tied the validity of experimental tests directly to the principle of randomization, arguing that randomly allocating treatments to plots could simulate the independence required for valid inference. This innovation established randomization as the “physical basis of the validity of the test” and became Fisher’s first principle of experimental design.<ref name=":1" />

Fisher went on to integrate randomization with two further principles, replication and blocking, to form a general framework for designing experiments. These ideas, first applied to agricultural trials, were presented systematically in ''The Design of Experiments'', helping to formalize experimental design as a statistical discipline.<ref name=":1" />

==Origin of the Null Hypothesis and the Lady Tasting Tea==
One of the most notable sections of the book describes the origin of the [[null hypothesis]]. Fisher illustrated it with a wager, a woman claimed to be able to tell whether milk or tea had been poured first into a cup.<ref name=":0" /> In order to test this, Fisher designed an experiment in which she was presented with eight cups, four of each preparation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fisher |first=R. A. |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.502684/page/n266/mode/1up |title=The Design of Experiments |date=January 1, 1935 |publisher=Oliver & Boyd Ltd. |isbn= |edition=1st |location=Edinburgh |pages=28 |language=en}}</ref> This came to be known as the [[Lady tasting tea|Lady tasting tea experiment]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fisher |first=R. A. |title=The World of Mathematics |orig-date=1956 |publisher=Dover Publications |year=2000 |isbn=9780486411514 |editor-last=Newman |editor-first=James Roy |edition=Unabridged, reprint |volume=3 |location=New York |publication-date=September 18, 2000 |pages=1512–1522 |language=en |chapter=Part 8: Mathematics of a Lady Tasting Tea |chapter-url=https://verso.mat.uam.es/~amparo.baillo/MatEstI/Mathematics%20of%20a%20lady%20tasting%20tea.pdf}}</ref> He defined the [[null hypothesis]] as the assumption that she has no such ability to make the distinction, meaning her answers would be due to chance. Under this assumption, the probability of guessing all eight cups correctly was calculated to be 1/70. Fisher argued that if she succeeded to distinguish whether milk or tea had been poured first into a cup, the null hypothesis could be rejected. Fisher stated “the null hypothesis is never proved or established, but is possibly disproved, in the course of experimentation. Every experiment may be said to exist only in order to give the facts a chance of disproving the null hypothesis,”<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Fisher |first=R. A. |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.502684/page/n265/mode/1up |title=The Design of Experiments |date=January 1, 1935 |publisher=Oliver & Boyd Ltd. |edition=1st |location=Edinburgh |pages=19 |language=en}}</ref> thus the concept of a null hypothesis was born. This discussion became central to the philosophy of [[statistical inference]].<ref name=":7" />

=== Further Developments in Experimental Designs ===
Beyond establishing the principles of [[randomization]], [[Replication (statistics)|replication]] and [[Blocking (statistics)|blocking]], ''The Design of Experiments'' advanced the statistical understanding of error estimation in field trials.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Yates |first=F. |date=June 1964 |title=Sir Ronald Fisher and the Design of Experiments |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2528399?origin=crossref |journal=Biometrics |publisher=International Biometric Society |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=307–321 |doi=10.2307/2528399 |via=JSTOR|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Before Fisher’s work, agricultural experiments often lacked a coherent theory for estimating experimental error, except in the simplest comparisons. Fisher formalized this process, allowing errors to be estimated directly from the data rather than assumed. His methods revealed the unreliability of earlier experiments that failed to account for natural variability, such as differences in soil fertility.<ref name=":2" /> Later editions of his related work, ''[[Statistical Methods for Research Workers]]'', introduced further refinements, including the analysis of [[covariance]], a technique developed to improve precision by adjusting for variation.<ref name=":2" /> Together, these innovations helped organize earlier agricultural practices into a coherent framework for experimental design and analysis.

== Controversies ==
Fisher has faced multiple criticisms and controversies through his decades-long career. His work had established a foundation for significance testing that stressed the indication of evidence against the [[null hypothesis]], using [[p-value]]s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Morgan |first=P. L. |date=2003 |title=Null Hypothesis Significance Testing: Philosophical and Practical Considerations of a Statistical Controversy |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15327035EX1104_2 |journal=Exceptionality |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=209–221 |doi=10.1207/S15327035EX1104_2 |via=Taylor & Francis Online|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Ronald Fisher argued that [[Inductive reasoning|inductive inference]] was crucial to the progression of scientific knowledge and that this is “experimentally demonstrable when we know how to conduct an experiment which will rarely fail to give us a statistically significant result.”<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fisher |first=R. A. |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.502684/page/n30/mode/1up?q=experimentally+demonstrable |title=The Design Of Experiments |date=January 1, 1935 |publisher=Oliver & Boyd Ltd. |edition=1st |location=Edinburgh |pages=16 |language=en}}</ref> Skeptics, such as Paul L. Morgan and [[Jacob Cohen (statistician)|Jacob Cohen]], expressed that there were considerable irregularities in Fisher's disagreements with [[probability]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=J. |date=1994 |title=The earth is round (p < .05). |url=https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.49.12.997 |journal=American Psychologist |language=en |volume=49 |issue=12 |pages=997–1003 |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.49.12.997 |via=APA PsycNet|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Cohen had a specific critique regarding Fisher, “who emphatically rejected [[Bayesian probability|Bayesian theory]] of inverse probability but slipped into invalid Bayesian interpretations of NHST [null hypothesis significance testing].”<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=J. |date=1994 |title=The earth is round (p < .05) |url=https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2F0003-066X.49.12.997 |journal=American Psychologist |volume=49 |issue=12 |pages=999 |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.49.12.997 |via=APA PsycNet}}</ref> Despite Fisher’s statistical legacy, the discourse has argued that his study has contributed to the extensive misinterpretation of [[Null hypothesis significance testing|NHST]] in modern research.<ref name=":4" />

In addition to critiques of his work, Fisher has been known to be controversial due to his views on race and history of supporting [[Eugenics|eugenic]] policies.<ref name=":4" />

== Legacy ==
[[File:Ronald Fisher.jpg|thumb|The founding father of ''The Design of Experiments'', Ronald A. Fisher, at the time of his scientific research in the 1930s.]]
After Fisher’s death in 1962, the methods of experimental design and analysis he had established decades earlier had transformed research across the physical, biological and statistical sciences.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Stanley |first=J. C. |date=1966 |title=The Influence of Fisher's "The Design of Experiments" on Educational Research Thirty Years Later |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/00028312003003223 |journal=American Educational Research Journal |language=en |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=223–229 |doi=10.3102/00028312003003223 |issn= |via=SageJournals|url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''The Design of Experiments'' (1935) and its later editions provided a systematic account of the logic of experimentation, as well as the formulation of the [[null hypothesis]] into a unified framework for scientific use.<ref name=":0" /> The book advanced the use of [[Factorial experiment|factorial designs]], which allowed researchers to study multiple factors and their interactions simultaneously.<ref name=":5" /> While ideas of combining treatments in this way was not entirely new, Fisher demonstrated its logical and statistical advantage over older approaches that favoured observation of one factor at a time.<ref name=":5" /> His framework later influenced fields such as [[psychology]] and [[education]], where experimental designs gradually replaced purely [[correlation]]al studies.<ref name=":5" /> Fisher’s concepts of [[randomization]], [[Error analysis (mathematics)|error analysis]], and [[statistical inference]] remain foundational.<ref name=":6" />

=== Impact of Fisher's Book and Research ===
In ''The Design of Experiments'', Ronald A. Fisher has made noteworthy inputs within the field of [[genetics]] and biological [[assay]]. The book discusses his study of systematically arranged experiments which demonstrated and fully articulated the incorrect assumptions about the independence of plot errors that can be properly eliminated using the process of [[randomization]].<ref name=":2" /> This is now commonly known as the principle of [[randomization]].

Since laying the groundwork in experimental design and analysis, many of Fisher’s initial works were advanced by other notable researchers, such as [[Frank Yates]].<ref name=":2" /> [[Rothamsted Research]] was particularly fond of developing the newer concepts of experimental design and analysis. Fisher’s studies have advanced sampling methods for experimental plots, effectively modernizing yield estimates in [[agriculture]] and survey methods in a variety of fields.<ref name=":2" /> By 1939, studies involving highly variable data had included these strategies which were adapted by [[agronomists]] worldwide.<ref name=":2" /> Decades after its publication, ''The Design of Experiments'' continues to shape modern research methodology.<ref name=":2" />
